content:
Numbers 15 closes with two events that at first may seem separate, yet they are closely connected. First, we meet a man who deliberately broke Yahweh's Sabbath command. Then God commanded Israel to wear tassels on their garments, so that they would remember His commandments and obey them. This follows naturally from what we studied before, for Numbers 15 had just dealt with unintentional sin, and then warned about deliberate, defiant sin. Now these closing verses immediately give us a real and living example of such serious disobedience, followed by God's gracious help against it.

While Israel was still in the wilderness, some people found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day (Numbers 15:32). Scripture tells us exactly what he was doing, but it does not tell us why he was doing it. Perhaps the sticks were meant as firewood for cooking, or for heating, or for some other work. What matters is that he deliberately went out gathering wood on the very day Yahweh had commanded Israel to rest. Now why was gathering sticks so serious a matter? It was because God had already made the Sabbath command completely clear. At Sinai He had said, "The seventh day is the Sabbath of Yahweh your God. In it you shall do no work" (Exodus 20:10). Even before Sinai, when the manna was given, Yahweh had instructed the people to gather what they needed beforehand, because the seventh day was a Sabbath of rest (Exodus 16:22-30). Later He specifically commanded, "You shall kindle no fire throughout your dwellings on the Sabbath day" (Exodus 35:3). So, this was not a man innocently doing something without knowing God's command.

He belonged to a people who had been taught again and again that the seventh day was holy to Yahweh. And this incident comes immediately after the warning against sinning "with a high hand," which makes his action especially solemn.

Those who found him gathering sticks brought him to Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation. Numbers 15:34 says, "They put him under guard, because it had not been explained what should be done to him." This does not mean they did not know that Sabbath-breaking was serious, for Exodus 31:14-15 had already prescribed death for deliberate Sabbath violation. Rather, in this particular case they did not presume to carry out judgment on their own.

They held the man in custody and waited for God's direction. Then Yahweh spoke clearly to Moses, "The man must surely be put to death; all the congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp" (Numbers 15:35). The congregation obeyed God's judgment. The severity of it shows us how seriously Yahweh regarded deliberate contempt for His covenant command. This was not a small matter of a few sticks. It was open, knowing rebellion against the word of the God who had redeemed them.

Centuries later, when Christ came, some of the Jewish religious leaders accused Him of breaking the Sabbath. But we must carefully distinguish their interpretation of the Sabbath from God's Law itself. Christ did not behave at all like the man in Numbers 15. That man knowingly performed forbidden work against Yahweh's command. But Christ healed the sick, showed mercy, and defended lawful acts of necessity. When His disciples plucked heads of grain because they were hungry, the Pharisees accused them of doing what was unlawful on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:1-8). Christ answered them from Scripture, He asked, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill?" (Mark 3:4). Christ was not rebelling against His Father's Law.

He was exposing the man-made interpretations that had misunderstood the true purpose of the Sabbath. He Himself said, "I have kept My Father's commandments" (John 15:10). So the Sabbath-breaker of Numbers 15 and the healing Christ did stand in complete contrast, the one in knowing rebellion, the other in perfect obedience.

Immediately after the death of the Sabbath-breaker, Yahweh gave Israel another command. He told Moses, "Speak to the children of Israel: Tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a blue thread in the tassels of the corners" (Numbers 15:38). These tassels were not merely decoration. God explained their purpose Himself, saying, "You shall have the tassel, that you may look upon it and remember all the commandments of Yahweh and do them" (Numbers 15:39). Israel wore garments with corners, and upon those corners God commanded them to place tassels, each with a blue cord. As they went through ordinary life, these tassels became visible reminders that they belonged to Yahweh and lived under His commandments. When they walked, worked, travelled, or went about their daily business, they carried upon their own clothing a quiet reminder: remember what Yahweh has spoken.

The command becomes even more meaningful when we notice exactly where Yahweh placed it. A man had just died because he knowingly disregarded God's command. And immediately afterward, God gave the whole nation something they could continually see that would remind them to obey. Forgetfulness could so easily lead to disobedience, and repeated disobedience could slowly harden into rebellion. So God, in His mercy, gave them a visible reminder to keep before their eyes. But God says something even deeper here. The tassels were to remind Israel not to "follow the harlotry to which your own heart and your own eyes are inclined" (Numbers 15:39). Their real problem was not simply that their memory was weak. It was that their own hearts and their own eyes could pull them away from Yahweh. They needed to remember continually whose people they were, and whose voice they were bound to obey.

And so the chapter ends with these words, "That you may remember and do all My commandments, and be holy for your God. I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to be your God: I am Yahweh your God" (Numbers 15:40-41). Notice how God brings Israel right back to their redemption. He had delivered them out of Egypt, and therefore they belonged entirely to Him. Their obedience was not to be a cold duty. It was to flow out of remembering the God who had redeemed them. The Sabbath command, and now these tassels, were both intended to keep Israel living under God's rule and remembering the God who had brought them out of Egypt. So Numbers 15 ends with a powerful movement: the commandment, then deliberate disobedience, then judgment, and finally a visible reminder to remember and obey. The man gathering sticks shows us the seriousness of knowingly disregarding God's Word. The tassels show us Yahweh graciously giving His people a continual reminder, so that His commandments would always remain before their eyes. Tomorrow, Yahweh willing, we will look more closely at these tassels, at the blue thread, at where they were placed and how they were worn, and at what this command teaches us in greater detail.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God and our Redeemer, who brought Your people out of Egypt to be Your own,
We see how seriously You regard the knowing rejection of Your command.

Guard us from following the wandering of our own hearts and the desire of our own eyes.

Set reminders before us, that we may remember Your Word in the middle of ordinary life.

Let our obedience flow not from cold duty, but from remembering the God who redeemed us.

Make us holy for You, for You are Yahweh our God, and we belong wholly to You.

"Oh, that my actions would consistently reflect your decrees!" - Psalm 119:5

In Christ name, we pray. Amen.
